questions.question: What is a coffee bean, anatomically speaking?
options: A. A dried seed extracted from a grass-like plant
B. The seed inside the fruit (cherry) of the Coffea plant
C. A type of legume bean closely related to soybeans
D. The dried outer skin of the coffee cherry
questions.explanation: A coffee bean is the seed of the coffee cherry — the small, red or yellow fruit that grows on the Coffea plant. There are typically two seeds per cherry, lying flat against each other inside the fruit.

questions.question: Compared to Robusta (Coffea canephora), Arabica coffee (Coffea arabica) generally:
options: A. Contains more caffeine and grows at lower altitudes
B. Is hardier, higher-yielding, and earthier in flavor
C. Contains less caffeine, grows at higher altitudes, and has more complex flavor
D. Is primarily used for instant coffee and mass-market espresso blends
questions.explanation: Arabica has lower caffeine than robusta (roughly half), grows at higher altitudes (1,000–2,000m), and produces more complex, fruity, and floral flavor profiles. Robusta is hardier, higher-yielding, and is commonly used in instant coffee and espresso blends for body and cost.

questions.question: Green coffee beans should be roasted quickly after purchase because they go stale within a few weeks, just like roasted beans.
questions.explanation: Green coffee beans can be stored for up to a year in proper conditions (cool, dark, dry environment) without significant quality loss. This is one of the practical advantages of home roasting — you can buy green coffee in bulk and roast small batches on demand, always ensuring your roasted coffee is fresh.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a compound found in green coffee that roasting will transform into flavor?
options: A. Sucrose and other reducing sugars
questions.explanation: Green coffee contains sugars, amino acids, chlorogenic acids, lipids, and water — all of which are transformed by the heat of roasting. Carbon monoxide is not a precursor compound in green coffee; CO₂ (carbon dioxide) is released during and after roasting, but carbon monoxide is not a relevant component.

questions.question: You receive a bag of green coffee and notice that some beans have turned black and others smell slightly musty. What might this indicate, and what would you do?
questions.sample_answer: Black beans typically indicate over-fermentation — a defect that occurred during processing. A musty smell suggests possible moisture damage or mold during storage. Both are quality problems. I would pick out the visibly black beans before roasting, as even a small number can negatively affect the flavor of the entire batch. If most of the bag smells musty, it may be a sign that the green coffee was improperly stored and the whole lot might be compromised.

questions.question: A 'peaberry' is a defective coffee bean and should always be discarded.
questions.explanation: A peaberry forms when only one seed develops inside the coffee cherry instead of two. The single seed grows rounder than a typical flat-sided bean. Peaberries are not defective — many roasters and consumers prize them for their even, round shape, which some believe leads to more uniform roasting. They are often sold as a specialty product at a premium.
